title: Zero-days with no disclosure window: what happened, what we learned, and what it means for responsible disclosure
summary: In the week of November 9, vulnerabilities in N-central were made public before we had a chance to fix them. There was no advance notice and no coordinated disclosure window,...
body_markdown:
In the week of November 9, vulnerabilities in N-central were made public before we had a chance to fix them. There was no advance notice and no coordinated disclosure window, so we made decisions in real time. We took our hosted servers offline, shipped a series of hotfixes, and kept customers informed of what was fixed and what was not. This post covers what happened, what we learned, and why the way flaws reach vendors matters more as attackers get faster.


## What happened


Two publications landed within four days. Neither followed a responsible disclosure process, so we had no advance notice and no coordinated fix window.


Date Event


Nov 9 First publication: N-central unauthenticated internet-facing flaws plus authenticated and privileged data leakage. We took hosted servers offline and advised customers to do the same


Nov 10 2026.4 HF2 released, fixing all internet-facing and unauthenticated issues. Hosted servers brought back online


Nov 12 Second publication: Legacy API abuse and Agent Impersonation – Legacy API had been defaulted to off for all customers for more than a year.


Nov 16 2026.4 HF3 released: stronger authentication and permission checks, hardened agent, probe and appliance communication, Legacy API removed completely


Nov 20 HF4 released: Remote Control (RDP) and Intune issues fixed and both services restored, plus an AlmaLinux Java package update


## How we triaged


Starting November 9, we responded to a series of zero-day vulnerabilities that were not responsibly disclosed. We sorted every issue by severity and exploitability and fixed the highest-risk ones first.


The first publication (November 9) fell into three tiers:


1. Internet-facing and unauthenticated.
2. Data leakage that requires authenticated access.
3. Data leakage that requires privileged authenticated access (Product Admin).


Tier 1 is the one that forced a hard call. An unauthenticated, internet-facing flaw in a management platform is exploitable by anyone who can reach the server, so we took our hosted servers offline and recommended that customers do the same. Once HF2 shipped, we brought our servers back online and recommended customers follow.


Tiers 2 and 3 carry lower exploitability because an attacker first needs valid credentials, including 2FA. Tier 3 is lower still: an attacker holding Product Admin credentials can already use the product itself for malicious actions, which is a larger risk than reading system settings.


## What was disclosed


The first publication (November 9) covered unauthenticated, internet-facing flaws and two tiers of data leakage that require authenticated or Product Admin access. The second (November 12) covered Legacy API abuse, which only affected customers who had explicitly turned on a feature that is off by default, and Agent Impersonation, which requires an attacker to already hold a foothold on an endpoint.


Fix-level detail, including every CVE, is already public: see the[vulnerability remediation update](https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-remediation-update) , the[HF2 release notes](https://status.n-able.com/2026/11/10/n-central-2026-4-hf2-release-notes/) and the[HF3 release notes](https://status.n-able.com/2026/11/14/n-central-2026-4-hf3-release-notes/) . This post does not repeat it.


Across Hotfixes 1 to 3 we fixed 27 CVEs: 3 in Hotfix 1 (October AlmaLinux OS updates), 7 in Hotfix 2 and 17 in Hotfix 3. Hotfix 4 fixed one more and restored the services we had disabled.


## Where things stand


Hotfix 4 closed out the precautionary measures. Remote Control (RDP) issues were fixed and the service restored, and the Intune issues were fixed and the integration restored. It also included an AlmaLinux Java package update that fixed one more CVE.


Hotfix 4 shipped on November 20. We are now focused on the remaining areas that were not responsibly disclosed, including the data leakage that requires Product Admin access, and we plan to cover the remaining vulnerabilities in the December release.


We are also shipping changes to shrink the exposed surface. Planned for Q1 2027: separate ports for agents, integrations and the console, an allow list of approved IP addresses for the UI and API, and the ability to run all of N-central behind a web application firewall. Login through N-able Login with Entra ID authentication only is planned for December 2026. We are also moving to a monthly update release that carries security fixes and bugfixes on a predictable schedule.


For current status and what to apply, see the[vulnerability remediation update](https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-remediation-update) .


## What we learned


1. **Triage by exploitability, not by count.** Sorting issues by who can reach them let us fix the unauthenticated, internet-facing class first and take a clear decision on hosted servers.
2. **Taking systems offline is a legitimate first move.** When a flaw is exploitable by anyone with network access and no fix exists, removing exposure beats waiting. We did it for our hosted servers and recommended customers do the same.
3. **Safe defaults did real work.** The Legacy API was off by default, so customers who never enabled it were protected. Required 2FA also lowered the risk of the authenticated classes.
4. **Precautionary disablement has a cost.** Disabling Remote Control and the Intune integration reduced risk but removed functionality our partners rely on. Hotfix 4 restored both once they were remediated.
5. **Publish in risk order and say what is still broken.** Naming known issues in each update lets partners make their own decisions while we finish.


## What this means for responsible disclosure


Responsible disclosure exists so a fix can ship before attackers can use a flaw. A vendor gets a private report and a reasonable window, and the public gets details once customers can protect themselves. Both publications last week skipped that step. Publishing a flaw before a fix exists is not responsible disclosure. It gives attackers the details before defenders have a patch, and it puts customers at risk for no one’s benefit.


The industry is debating how fast details should go public now that AI speeds up both discovery and exploitation. Google Project Zero has announced it will cut its disclosure window from 90 days to 30 days by 2028. We welcome that pressure, and vendors should be fixing faster. But even the most aggressive policy keeps a window, however short, for the vendor to build a fix before details are published. In this case the window was zero.


The cost showed up in concrete decisions. We had to choose between keeping hosted servers online and protecting them, and we had to ask customers to make the same choice before a patch existed. A coordinated window would have let us release HF2 and HF3 first.


What we would ask of the industry:


- **Report privately first.** Send findings to the vendor’s security contact and allow time to fix.
- **Publish after a fix exists.** Details released alongside a patch protect customers instead of exposing them.
- **Credit good-faith research.** The HF2 fix for CVE-2026-125882 credits Nate Fair of Sprocket Security, which shows the process working.
- **Vendors owe researchers a clear path.** A visible reporting channel and fast acknowledgement make the responsible route the easy one.


Our PSIRT has run coordinated disclosure for years. Researchers report through an online form, and we acknowledge every report within 48 hours, validate the issue, score it with CVSS 3.1 plus context, and mitigate before disclosure. Remediation takes as little as 24 hours and up to 30 days depending on the issue. Researchers are recognized in our Hall of Fame, and good-faith research under our policy has safe harbor under the CFAA and DMCA. We have run a bug bounty since May 2022, and our invitation-only program pays vetted researchers across five products.[N-able Vulnerability Disclosure Program](https://www.n-able.com/security-and-privacy/vulnerability-disclosure-program)


## How we build and test


A week like this raises a fair question: what was already in place? Since 2021 we have built a company-wide secure engineering program of standards, people, automated controls and independent validation, and we strengthen it every year. It has matured in stages: policy foundation in 2021, tooling and standards in 2022, a Secure Engineering Standard in 2023, Secure by Design and a champions network in 2024 and 2025, and in 2026 AI-assisted work combined with human review.


The program runs through five stages of every release.


The last step matters most this week. Findings become standards, tests and guardrails, so each issue we close makes the next release harder to break in the same way.


## How AI-powered red and blue teams find and fix defects


Frontier models increase attacker capability. They also dramatically increase how quickly we can discover, validate, and eliminate weaknesses. We use AI tools on both sides of the work, with expert people keeping judgment and accountability.


Our AI-powered red team thinks like the attacker:


- Discover. Use frontier models and attacker tooling to search broadly across code, APIs and infrastructure.
- Chain. Connect individual weaknesses into realistic attack paths and challenge assumptions.
- Prove. Reproduce findings, establish exploitability and give Engineering actionable evidence.


Our AI-powered blue team defends, validates and learns:


- Harden. Convert proven attack paths into code fixes, guardrails and stronger default controls.
- Validate. Use AI-assisted analysis, telemetry, and targeted retesting to confirm the weakness is closed.
- Learn. Feed findings into detection, response, architecture standards and the secure development lifecycle.


Together, the teams run a continuous adversarial loop: discover, prove, harden, validate, learn. AI expands breadth and speed. Expert red and blue teams to preserve judgment, prove impact and drive durable remediation.


## Independent testing


We also do not rely on our own view of our code. Independent third parties test all of N-able’s products at three levels of knowledge:


- **White box, full source access.** Independent experts review source code, architecture, and known findings to identify deep design and implementation weaknesses using AI tools.
- **Grey box, realistic foothold.** Testers start with limited access, such as a product trial, ordinary credentials, or an installation image, then try to expand it.
- **Black box, external attacker view.** Continuous automated penetration testing challenges public production interfaces with no internal knowledge or privileged access.


Findings from all three are tracked through remediation and retest. None of this means the work is done. It means we can put the lessons from this week straight back into the program.


## Why AI raises the stakes


Whether or not AI played a part in these disclosures, the direction of travel is clear. AI tooling lowers the cost of finding flaws in large codebases and of turning a finding into a working exploit. That compresses the time between discovery and attack, and it makes the disclosure window more valuable, not less.


Three implications follow for vendors and researchers:


- **Patch windows get shorter.** If discovery is faster, a fix that takes weeks leaves a larger gap. Our week of hotfixes is the pace vendors should be ready to match.
- **Report volume will rise.** AI-assisted research will produce more findings, including noise. Vendors need triage that separates exploitable, unauthenticated issues from lower-risk ones, which is the approach we took in this response.
- **Defenders need the same tools.** Attackers will use AI to scale. Defenders have to use it to triage alerts, correlate signals and cut response time, while keeping a person accountable for the decisions that matter, such as taking a system offline. Our red and blue teams work this way as described above.


Responsible disclosure was designed for a world where finding and exploiting a flaw took time. As that time shrinks, the norms matter more: private reports, a fix first, then publication.


## The bottom line


Protecting our customers is the job, and security at N-able is a program, not a reaction. Every release passes through defined requirements, threat modeling, automated scanning, agentic review, penetration testing and a staged rollout. Every finding becomes a standard, a test or a guardrail, so the next release is stronger than the last.


Going forward we are doubling down on three things:


- **Independent testing at every level of access.** From full source review to continuous external testing, with findings tracked through remediation and retest.
- **Offense and defense working together.** Our red team uses frontier models to find weaknesses before attackers do. Our blue team validates fixes, expands detection and feeds lessons back into how we build.
- **Secure defaults.** Risky capabilities stay off unless a customer deliberately turns them on.


Our commitment to our partners and customers is simple. We find weaknesses first, fix them in order of risk, and tell you clearly what changed. That is how we keep the businesses that depend on us safe, and it is how we will keep earning their trust.
